1Why start here? The big idea

When an application feels slow, people tend to blame the query. But the query is only one small piece of a much bigger machine. The database sits inside a chain: application → SQL Server instance → virtual or physical hardware → disks → network. Any one of those links can be the real culprit.

That is the whole point of Chapter 1. Before you start tuning queries, you check whether the server was ever set up correctly in the first place. A surprising number of "mystery" performance problems turn out to be a bad setting somebody chose five years ago and never revisited.

In plain terms

Don't start by staring at a slow query. Start by asking: is this server built and configured sensibly? This chapter is the checklist for answering that question.

Hardware OS Virtualization SQL Server settings Database settings Monitoring overhead

2Hardware & operating system

The author deliberately avoids naming specific vendors or part numbers — hardware goes stale fast. Instead he gives rules that stay true.

CPUBuy the fastest CPU you can afford

SQL Server licensing usually costs more than the hardware itself. You could build a decent server for less than the retail price of four Enterprise Edition cores. So don't cheap out on the CPU — especially on Standard Edition, which caps how many cores you may use anyway.

  • Newer generation beats same-speed older generation — typically 10–15% free performance just from generation.
  • Fewer fast cores vs. many slow cores? OLTP (and especially In-Memory OLTP) likes fast single cores. Data warehouse / analytical workloads like more cores and parallelism.

Memory"How much does SQL Server need?" → "More."

More memory means more data cached, which means less disk I/O. Adding RAM is often the cheapest, fastest fix available.

  • Adding memory only hides bad queries — it doesn't fix them, and eventually the data outgrows the cache. Treat it as a temporary bandage, not a cure.
  • Edition limits matter: Standard Edition (2014+) caps the buffer pool at 128 GB, In-Memory OLTP at 32 GB per database, and columnstore segments at 32 GB. Web Edition gets half of that.
  • Don't forget memory for other components: plan cache, lock manager.

DiskLow latency is the whole game

SQL Server reads and writes constantly, so a fast disk subsystem is essential. The author's targets for critical tier-1 systems:

File typeTarget latencyWhy
Data file reads/writes3–5 msRandom I/O is constant; queues build fast
Transaction log writes1–2 msLog writes are synchronous — every commit waits
  • Measure latency inside SQL Server, not on the storage array. SQL Server's numbers are routinely higher than storage KPIs because of queueing.
  • Priority order if you have performance tiers: tempdb first, then transaction log, then data files.
  • Putting several log and/or data files on one drive turns sequential writes into random I/O — avoid it.
  • Split data and log onto separate physical drives for maintainability and recovery — but check the storage config first, since splitting LUNs on an array without enough spindles can make things worse.
  • The author does not split clustered and nonclustered indexes across filegroups onto different drives — it rarely helps I/O and it badly complicates disaster recovery.

NetworkYour throughput equals your slowest hop

A 10 Gbps server uplink is meaningless if there's a 1 Gbps switch in the path. When troubleshooting network performance, map the whole topology. This matters most for network-based storage — keep the I/O path to disks as direct as possible.

On clusters: a dedicated heartbeat network for AlwaysOn Failover Clusters / Availability Groups is good practice on simple single-subnet setups. In complex multi-subnet or virtual environments, extra networks can create routing problems instead of solving them.

OS & appsKeep it clean and current

  • Use the most recent OS version that supports your SQL Server, and patch both on a regular schedule.
  • On SQL Server versions before 2016, use the 64-bit build — it scales better.
  • Since SQL Server 2017, Linux is a first-class option; performance is similar to Windows, but HA strategy differs (e.g. Pacemaker instead of Windows Server Failover Cluster).
  • Use a dedicated database host. App servers are cheap and easy to scale; database hosts are not.
  • Don't run SSMS on the server in an RDP session — work remotely instead.
  • If antivirus is mandatory, exclude database folders from scanning.

Virtualization & cloudFine — but watch the host

Virtualize unless you genuinely need every last ounce of bare-metal performance. You gain vMotion / Live Migration as an extra HA layer, easier hardware upgrades, and simpler management. Overhead grows on very large many-core servers, but is usually acceptable.

The catch

The guest VM's own metrics can look perfectly healthy while the host is over-provisioned. Work with your infrastructure engineers, check physical vs. allocated vCPU and RAM on the host, and reserve resources for mission-critical SQL Server VMs. Once you're past this layer, troubleshooting a VM is the same as troubleshooting physical hardware — and the cloud is just someone else's datacenter.

3Configuring the SQL Server instance

The default setup is "relatively decent" for light and moderate workloads, but several things need validating.

First command to runVersion and patch level

First statement in any health checkT-SQL
SELECT @@VERSION;

Why bother? Two reasons: it reveals the patching discipline of the environment, and it tells you which known bugs may already be fixed in a service pack or cumulative update you haven't applied. The author has repeatedly been called in to fix problems that were already solved by a patch.

Upgrading is often the highest-value "tuning" you can do. Moving from SQL Server 2012 to 2016 or later commonly gives 20–40% performance improvement with no other changes. Since 2016 SP1, many former Enterprise-only features (like data compression) also work in lower editions. Always test before upgrading — risk is small for minor patches, higher for major upgrades.

Setting #1Instant File Initialization (IFI)

Normally, when SQL Server grows a file it fills the new space with zeros first. That blocks every session writing to that file and spikes I/O. For transaction logs this is unavoidable. For data files you can skip it.

Enable IFI by granting SA_MANAGE_VOLUME_NAME (the "Perform Volume Maintenance Task" privilege) to the SQL Server startup account via secpol.msc, then restart the service. From SQL Server 2016 onward you can grant it right in the setup wizard.

Check it on SQL Server 2012 SP4 / 2016 SP1 or later:

Quick check via DMVT-SQL
SELECT instant_file_initialization_enabled, *
FROM sys.dm_server_services;

On older versions, use the trace-flag trick from the book — create a dummy database and read what the error log says about zeroing:

Listing 1-1 — Checking IFI in older SQL Server versionsT-SQL
DBCC TRACEON(3004,3605,-1);
GO
CREATE DATABASE Dummy;
GO
EXEC sp_readerrorlog 0,1,N'Dummy';
GO
DROP DATABASE Dummy;
GO
DBCC TRACEOFF(3004,3605,-1);
GO

If IFI is off, the log shows zeroing of both the .mdf and the .ldf. If it's on, only the .ldf is zeroed.

The trade-off

IFI has a small security implication: a DBA could potentially read remnants of previously deleted files through newly allocated data pages. Most systems accept that risk — if yours does, turn IFI on.

Setting #2tempdb

tempdb stores temporary objects for users and for SQL Server itself. It is extremely busy and a classic contention point.

  • Put it on the fastest drive. It doesn't need redundancy or persistence (it's recreated at startup), so local SSD or cloud ephemeral storage is ideal — but remember SQL Server goes down if tempdb disappears.
  • On non-Enterprise editions, if the server has more RAM than SQL Server can consume, tempdb can live on a RAM drive. Never do this on Enterprise — that memory is better spent on the buffer pool. Pre-allocate the files to the RAM drive's full size and add small on-disk files as overflow.
  • Always use multiple data files. Rule of thumb:
CPU corestempdb data files
8 or fewerOne per core
More than 88, or ¼ of the cores — whichever is greater, rounded up in batches of 4
Example: 24 cores8 files
Example: 40 cores12 files

Give every tempdb file the same initial size and auto-growth set in MB, never percent — that's what lets SQL Server balance usage evenly.

Setting #3Trace flags

Trace flags toggle hidden product behaviors. Check which ones are already on with DBCC TRACESTATUS; enable new ones in SQL Server Configuration Manager or via the -T startup parameter.

FlagWhat it doesVerdict
T1118Stops mixed-extent allocations, reducing tempdb catalog contentionEnable on 2014 and earlier. Unnecessary on 2016+ (default behavior).
T1117Auto-grows every file in a filegroup when one fills up, balancing I/OOptional on 2014 and earlier for tempdb. Check for unevenly sized filegroups first.
T2371Makes the statistics-update threshold dynamic instead of the fixed 20%-of-rows rule, so big tables get updated statsEnable unless every database is compatibility level 130+.
T3226Stops logging successful backups to the error logHandy for keeping logs small and readable.
T1222Writes deadlock graphs to the error logRemove it — redundant with the system_health xEvents session, and it makes logs harder to read.
T4199Enables Query Optimizer hotfixes from service packs / CUsGenerally avoid in production — raises plan-regression risk after patching unless you can regression-test thoroughly.
T7412Lightweight query profiling (2016/2017)Cheap execution-plan and metrics collection; covered further in Chapter 5.
Short version

On SQL Server 2014 and earlier: enable T1118, T2371, and maybe T1117. On 2016+: enable T2371 unless all databases sit at compatibility level 130 or above. Then audit every other flag — third-party tools quietly install some, and they can hurt performance.

Server optionOptimize for Ad-hoc Workloads

By default SQL Server caches the full execution plan of every ad-hoc (unparameterized) query. Most ad-hoc queries never run a second time, so that's wasted plan-cache memory. Turn this setting on and SQL Server caches only a tiny plan stub (a few hundred bytes) on first execution, promoting it to a full plan only if the query comes back.

Recommendation

Enable it on every system. Costs nothing but the occasional extra compile of a genuinely repeated query. It doesn't affect parameterized queries or stored procedures. On SQL Server 2019 / Azure SQL Database you can also set it per-database with OPTIMIZE_FOR_AD_HOC_WORKLOADS.

Server optionMax Server Memory

Controls how much memory SQL Server may use. There's endless debate about the "right" formula, and it's true that a wrong value is worse than the default. But the author's experience says the most common problem is severe under-provisioning: someone upgraded the hardware and forgot to raise the limit, or calculated it wrongly on a shared server. Raising it (or temporarily resetting to default) can produce instant wins. Chapter 7 covers the details.

Server optionAffinity mask & NUMA

On multi-NUMA hardware (usually one NUMA node per physical CPU), if you restrict SQL Server to fewer cores than the machine has, spread those cores evenly across NUMA nodes. Limiting 24 cores on two 18-core Xeons: take 12 + 12, not 18 + 6.

Listing 1-2 — Checking scheduler (CPU) distribution across NUMA nodesT-SQL
SELECT
  parent_node_id
  ,COUNT(*) as [Schedulers]
  ,SUM(current_tasks_count) as [Current]
  ,SUM(runnable_tasks_count) as [Runnable]
FROM sys.dm_os_schedulers
WHERE status = 'VISIBLE ONLINE'
GROUP BY parent_node_id;

Compare the Schedulers count per parent_node_id — an even split across nodes is what you want.

Server optionParallelism (MAXDOP & cost threshold)

The defaults (MAXDOP = 0, cost threshold 5) are relics and don't suit modern servers. Rules of thumb:

  • MAXDOP = ¼ of available CPUs on OLTP, ½ on data warehouse. Very large OLTP servers: keep it at 16 or below. Never exceed the number of schedulers in a single NUMA node.
  • Cost Threshold for Parallelism = 50.
  • SQL Server 2016+ / Azure SQL: set MAXDOP per database with ALTER DATABASE SCOPED CONFIGURATION SET MAXDOP when one instance hosts mixed workloads.

AuditWhich server settings were changed?

SQL Server won't tell you the defaults, so you have to hardcode them and compare against sys.configurations. Here's the book's approach (the published script lists a few settings; the full version is in the companion materials):

Listing 1-3 — Detecting changes in server configuration settingsT-SQL
DECLARE
    @defaults TABLE
    (
        name SYSNAME NOT NULL PRIMARY KEY,
        def_value SQL_VARIANT NOT NULL
    )
INSERT INTO @defaults(name,def_value)
VALUES('backup compression default',0);
INSERT INTO @defaults(name,def_value)
VALUES('cost threshold for parallelism',5);
INSERT INTO @defaults(name,def_value)
VALUES('max degree of parallelism',0);
INSERT INTO @defaults(name,def_value)
VALUES('max server memory (MB)',2147483647);
INSERT INTO @defaults(name,def_value)
VALUES('optimize for ad hoc workloads',0);
/* Other settings are omitted in the book */

SELECT
    c.name, c.description, c.value_in_use, c.value
    ,d.def_value, c.is_dynamic, c.is_advanced
FROM
    sys.configurations c JOIN @defaults d ON
        c.name = d.name
WHERE
    c.value_in_use <> d.def_value OR
    c.value <> d.def_value
ORDER BY
    c.name;

4Configuring your databases

Turn this offAuto Shrink

Auto Shrink periodically shrinks the database and hands free space back to the OS. Sounds tidy; isn't. The shrink works at the physical level — it finds empty space near the front of the file and moves allocated extents from the end into it, ignoring extent ownership. The result: heavy load and serious index fragmentation. And usually for nothing, because the files just grow again as data arrives.

Recommendation

Disable Auto Shrink and manage file space yourself. Same for transaction log files — never auto-shrink them.

Also turn offAuto Close

With Auto Close on, SQL Server throws away the database's buffer-pool pages and cached plans when the last connection closes. The next session pays for re-caching and recompiling. Disable it, with few exceptions (perhaps an instance hosting hundreds of rarely used databases).

Check theseOther database settings

SettingWhat you wantWhy
Page VerifyCHECKSUMDetects consistency errors far more effectively; helps resolve corruption cases
Recovery modelNot SIMPLE for critical DBsIn SIMPLE you cannot recover beyond the last full backup — a real data-loss risk. Raise it with stakeholders immediately.
Compatibility levelNewest level matching your SQL Server versionOlder levels block new features. But test first — going from 110 to 120+ switches on the new cardinality estimator and can change plans dramatically.

To de-risk a compatibility-level upgrade, keep the old cardinality estimator for a while: set LEGACY_CARDINALITY_ESTIMATION = ON (2016+) or enable trace flag T9481 (2014). That lets you change one thing at a time. Chapter 5 goes deeper.

Transaction logFewer, better-sized VLFs

SQL Server uses write-ahead logging and writes the log serially, "merry-go-round" style. It divides the log into Virtual Log Files (VLFs) and manages them as whole units — it cannot truncate a VLF that holds even one active record.

  • One log file is almost always enough. Multiple log files complicate admin and rarely help performance.
  • Too few huge VLFs → slow, awkward log management and truncation. Too many tiny VLFs → degraded log performance. Aim for no more than a few hundred VLFs in production.
  • Growth of 64 MB–1 GB creates ~8 VLFs; over 1 GB creates ~16. Percent-based growth is the enemy — it produces wildly uneven VLFs. The author grows in 1,024 MB chunks (yielding 128 MB VLFs) unless the log needs to be huge.
  • Count VLFs with sys.dm_db_log_info (2016+) or DBCC LOGINFO (older). If it's bad, rebuild the log: shrink to minimum, then grow in 1,024–4,096 MB chunks.
  • Don't cap the maximum size or disable auto-growth — you want emergency growth to work.
Counting VLFs (SQL Server 2016+)T-SQL
-- How many VLFs does this log have?
SELECT COUNT(*) AS [VLF_Count]
FROM sys.dm_db_log_info(DB_ID());

Data filesFilegroups and Proportional Fill

By default a new database gets one data file in PRIMARY and one log file. That's suboptimal for performance, management, and HA.

  • SQL Server tracks space through allocation maps. On volatile data these become contention points because access is serialized. Multiple files in the filegroup give you multiple sets of allocation pages and reduce that contention.
  • Proportional Fill writes mostly to the file with the most free space. Identically sized files with identical MB-based growth keep writes balanced.
  • Consider AUTOGROW_ALL_FILES (2016+) so every file in the filegroup grows together. On older versions trace flag T1117 does this — but server-wide.

When laying out (or re-laying out) filegroups, the author's guidance:

  1. Multiple data files in volatile-data filegroups — start with four, add more if latching issues appear. Same size, same MB growth, AUTOGROW_ALL_FILES on. Read-only filegroups need only one file.
  2. Don't spread clustered indexes, nonclustered indexes, or LOB data across filegroups — little gain, real pain during corruption recovery.
  3. Keep related tables together (e.g. Orders and OrderLineItems) — simpler management and disaster recovery.
  4. Keep PRIMARY empty if possible.

5Reading the error log

The SQL Server error log is another early stop in troubleshooting. Errors 823 and 824 in particular can point to disk subsystem problems or database corruption. The problem is noise: the log is full of informational messages that bury the real signal.

You can read it in SSMS, or programmatically with xp_readerrorlog. The book's script filters out the noise and, optionally, shows you the log lines around each error so you get context.

VariableControls
@StartDate / @EndDateThe time window to analyze
@NumErrorLogsHow many rolled-over log files to read
@ExcludeLogonErrorsDrops logon-auditing messages
@ShowSurroundingEventsAlso returns informational messages around each error
@SurroundingEventsBeforeSecond / ...AfterSecondThe context window, in seconds
@ErrorsToIgnorePatterns for known-harmless "error" lines

It produces two result sets: the cleaned-up list of errors, then (optionally) the surrounding context for each one.

Listing 1-4 — Analyzing the SQL Server error logT-SQL
IF OBJECT_ID('tempdb..#Logs',N'U') IS NOT NULL DROP TABLE #Logs;
IF OBJECT_ID('tempdb..#Errors',N'U') IS NOT NULL DROP TABLE #Errors;
GO
CREATE TABLE #Errors
(
  LogNum INT NULL,
  LogDate DATETIME NULL,
  ID INT NOT NULL IDENTITY(1,1),
  ProcessInfo VARCHAR(50) NULL,
  [Text] NVARCHAR(MAX) NULL,
  PRIMARY KEY(ID)
);
CREATE TABLE #Logs
(
  [LogDate] DATETIME NULL,
  ProcessInfo VARCHAR(50) NULL,
  [Text] NVARCHAR(MAX) NULL
);
DECLARE
  @StartDate DATETIME = DATEADD(DAY,-7,GETDATE())
  ,@EndDate DATETIME = GETDATE()
  ,@NumErrorLogs INT = 1
  ,@ExcludeLogonErrors BIT = 1
  ,@ShowSurroundingEvents BIT = 1
  ,@ExcludeLogonSurroundingEvents BIT = 1
  ,@SurroundingEventsBeforeSecond INT = 5
  ,@SurroundingEventsAfterSecond INT = 5
  ,@LogNum INT = 0;
DECLARE
  @ErrorsToIgnore TABLE
  (
    ErrorText NVARCHAR(1024) NOT NULL
  );
INSERT INTO @ErrorsToIgnore(ErrorText)
VALUES
  (N'Registry startup parameters:%'),
  (N'Logging SQL Server messages in file%'),
  (N'CHECKDB for database%finished without errors%');

WHILE (@LogNum <= @NumErrorLogs)
BEGIN
  INSERT INTO #Errors(LogDate,ProcessInfo,Text)
    EXEC [master].[dbo].[xp_readerrorlog]
      @LogNum, 1, N'error', NULL, @StartDate, @EndDate, N'desc';
  IF @@ROWCOUNT > 0
    UPDATE #Errors SET LogNum = @LogNum WHERE LogNum IS NULL;
  SET @LogNum += 1;
END;

IF @ExcludeLogonErrors = 1
  DELETE FROM #Errors WHERE ProcessInfo = 'Logon';

DELETE FROM e
FROM #Errors e
WHERE EXISTS
(
  SELECT *
  FROM @ErrorsToIgnore i
  WHERE e.Text LIKE i.ErrorText
);

-- Errors only
SELECT * FROM #Errors ORDER BY LogDate DESC;

IF @@ROWCOUNT > 0 AND @ShowSurroundingEvents = 1
BEGIN
  DECLARE
    @LogDate DATETIME
    ,@ID INT = 0

  WHILE 1 = 1
  BEGIN
    SELECT TOP 1 @LogNum = LogNum, @LogDate = LogDate, @ID = ID
    FROM #Errors
    WHERE ID > @ID
    ORDER BY ID;

    IF @@ROWCOUNT = 0
      BREAK;

    SELECT
      @StartDate = DATEADD(SECOND, -@SurroundingEventsBeforeSecond, @LogDate)
      ,@EndDate = DATEADD(SECOND, @SurroundingEventsAfterSecond, @LogDate);

    INSERT INTO #Logs(LogDate,ProcessInfo,Text)
      EXEC [master].[dbo].[xp_readerrorlog]
        @LogNum, 1, NULL, NULL, @StartDate, @EndDate;
  END;

  IF @ExcludeLogonSurroundingEvents = 1
    DELETE FROM #Logs WHERE ProcessInfo = 'Logon';

  DELETE FROM e
  FROM #Logs e
  WHERE EXISTS
  (
    SELECT *
    FROM @ErrorsToIgnore i
    WHERE e.Text LIKE i.ErrorText
  );

  SELECT * FROM #Logs ORDER BY LogDate DESC;
END

What you're looking for is system-specific, so the book doesn't enumerate every possible error. The rule is: investigate anything suspicious and understand its possible impact. Finally, if it isn't already done, set up SQL Server Agent alerts for high-severity errors.

6Putting too much on one server

Consolidation cuts hardware and licensing cost, but it isn't free. There's no universal strategy — weigh data volume, load, hardware, business and security requirements. A few firm rules:

  • Don't mix OLTP and data warehouse/reporting databases on one heavily loaded server. Warehouse queries churn through huge amounts of data, hammer I/O, and flush the buffer pool — hurting every other database on the instance. If they're already combined, consider splitting them.
  • Watch security features. Audit runs at the server level and adds overhead to everything. TDE is database-level, but if any database on the instance has it enabled, tempdb gets encrypted too — overhead for all.
  • As a general rule, don't keep databases with different security requirements on the same instance. Watch metric trends and split databases when needed.
Better approach

Instead of piling many independent active databases onto one SQL Server instance, virtualize — run several VMs on one or a few hosts. You get far better flexibility, manageability, and isolation, and resource consumption is much easier to control.

7The observer effect

Every serious production system needs monitoring — it makes you proactive and shortens incident detection and recovery. But monitoring costs you something, and sometimes the cost is large.

Two real examples from the author's consulting work:

  • A tool that called sys.dm_db_index_physical_stats in DETAILED mode for every index in the database every four hours. Result: enormous I/O spikes, a wiped buffer pool, and a visible performance hit.
  • A tool that constantly polled DMVs, adding significant CPU load.

Monitoring built from T-SQL is at least visible — you can find the queries and measure them. Extended Events monitoring is much harder to spot, and some events are genuinely heavy. The session below captures every query in the system, which is exactly the kind of thing that looks harmless on a slide and hurts on a busy box:

Listing 1-5 — Creating an xEvents session to capture queries in the systemT-SQL
CREATE EVENT SESSION CaptureQueries ON SERVER
ADD EVENT sqlserver.rpc_completed
(
  SET collect_statement=(1)
  ACTION
  (
    sqlos.task_time
    ,sqlserver.client_app_name
    ,sqlserver.client_hostname
    ,sqlserver.database_name
    ,sqlserver.nt_username
    ,sqlserver.sql_text
  )
),
ADD EVENT sqlserver.sql_batch_completed
(
  ACTION
  (
    sqlos.task_time
    ,sqlserver.client_app_name
    ,sqlserver.client_hostname
    ,sqlserver.database_name
    ,sqlserver.nt_username
    ,sqlserver.sql_text
  )
),
ADD EVENT sqlserver.sql_statement_completed
ADD TARGET package0.event_file
(SET FILENAME=N'C:\PerfLogs\LongSql.xel',MAX_FILE_SIZE=(200))
WITH
(
  MAX_MEMORY =4096 KB
  ,EVENT_RETENTION_MODE=ALLOW_SINGLE_EVENT_LOSS
  ,MAX_DISPATCH_LATENCY=5 SECONDS
);

Deployed on a heavily loaded server with lots of concurrent requests, the effect is measurable. The author tested throughput with and without the session — and found enabling it cut throughput by about 20%:

The lesson

Evaluate your monitoring strategy and estimate its overhead as part of the analysis — especially on servers hosting multiple databases. xEvents operates at the server level: filtering on database_id happens after the event fires, so it affects every database on the instance. Check for unnecessary monitoring and data-collection tools during every investigation.

8Key takeaways

Troubleshooting is a holistic process. You examine the hardware, OS, and virtualization layers, then the SQL Server and database configurations, and adjust what's wrong. The book's own closing summary boils down to this set of best practices that apply to most systems:

Chapter 2

SQL Server Execution Model and Wait Statistics

How SQL Server actually runs your queries — schedulers, workers, tasks — and the single most useful troubleshooting technique in the product: Wait Statistics.

Book pages 27–44 · 6 figures · 4 code listings

1Why you must understand the execution model

You cannot troubleshoot SQL Server without knowing how it runs work. If you don't know where a query actually spends its time, you're guessing. This chapter builds that mental model, then gives you the tool that turns the model into action.

The route is: architecture → SQLOS and scheduling → task states → Wait Statistics → the DMVs that expose it all → Resource Governor for keeping workloads apart.

In plain terms

A query is never "just running." At any instant it is either on a CPU, waiting for a CPU, or waiting for a resource (a disk page, a lock, memory, a network reply). If you measure which of those three it spends most of its time in — and for what — you have found your bottleneck. That measurement is Wait Statistics.

2SQL Server at a high level

SQL Server is dozens of components and subsystems. You don't need all of them — just five layers and the abstraction beneath them.

Layer 1Protocol layer

Handles talking to clients. It uses an internal format called Tabular Data Stream (TDS) over TCP/IP or Named Pipes; a client on the same machine can use Shared Memory instead.

Troubleshooting tip

When you chase a connectivity issue, check which protocols are actually enabled. Some editions — Express and Developer, for example — disable TCP/IP and Named Pipes by default, so they refuse all remote connections until you turn the protocols on in SQL Server Configuration Manager. This is a very common "the server is down!" false alarm.

Layer 2Query Processor

Responsible for query optimization and execution: it parses, optimizes, manages compiled plans, and orchestrates every aspect of running a query.

Layer 3Storage Engine

Everything to do with data on disk — data access, transaction log management, transactions, locking, and concurrency.

Layer 4In-Memory OLTP Engine

Handles memory-optimized tables: data management and access, native compilation, and persistence.

The glueQuery Interop, SQLOS, and PAL

  • Query Interop (not drawn in the figure) is what lets the Query Processor work with row-based and memory-optimized tables alike, transparently routing each request to the Storage Engine or the In-Memory OLTP Engine.
  • SQLOS is the most critical abstraction layer. It isolates everything above it from the OS and owns scheduling, resource management and monitoring, and exception handling. When a component needs memory it does not call the OS — it asks SQLOS. That's what gives SQL Server fine-grained control over its own execution without depending on the operating system's behaviour.
  • PAL (Platform Abstraction Layer), added with Linux support in SQL Server 2017, is the proxy between SQLOS and the OS. Except for a few performance-critical paths, SQLOS calls PAL rather than the OS directly — which keeps SQL Server's code nearly identical on Windows and Linux and speeds up development.
Windows vs. Linux

From a troubleshooting standpoint you'll see very little difference. Your OS-level analysis differs, but once you're inside SQL Server, both platforms behave identically — so the rest of the book doesn't distinguish between them.

3SQLOS and the execution model

A busy database server has far more active threads than CPUs, so scheduling is the whole game.

BackgroundWhy SQL Server stopped trusting the OS

Early SQL Server versions relied on Windows scheduling. But Windows and Linux are general-purpose OSes using preemptive scheduling: each thread gets a time quantum, then gets switched out. That switch is expensive — it bounces between user mode and kernel mode.

SQL Server 7.0 introduced User Mode Scheduler (UMS), a thin scheduling layer using cooperative scheduling: SQL Server threads voluntarily yield every 4 ms, letting others run. Far fewer expensive context switches. SQL Server 2005 rebuilt this into the much more robust SQLOS, which now also owns memory and I/O management, exception handling, and CLR / external-language hosting.

Exception to the rule

Some processes still run preemptively: extended stored procedures, CLR routines, external languages, and a few others. That's why you'll occasionally see PREEMPTIVE_* waits.

SchedulersOne per logical CPU, plus one

At startup SQLOS creates a set of schedulers that manage workload across CPUs. There is one per logical CPU, plus one extra for the Dedicated Admin Connection (DAC).

Worked example

Two quad-core physical CPUs with hyper-threading enabled = 16 logical CPUs = 17 schedulers (16 + 1 DAC).

  • For practical purposes, treat "scheduler" as "CPU" — the book uses the terms interchangeably.
  • The DAC is your last-resort connection when SQL Server is unresponsive and refuses normal connections (Chapter 13).
  • Each scheduler is ONLINE or OFFLINE depending on the affinity mask and core-based licensing. Schedulers usually stay put on a CPU, but can migrate under heavy load.

Workers & tasksThe two nouns that matter

Schedulers manage a pool of worker threads ("workers"), capped by Max Worker Threads. The default of 0 means SQL Server sizes the pool itself — don't change it unless you know exactly what you're doing.

ConceptWhat it isKey rules
WorkerLogical representation of an OS threadCreated when no idle worker is free; destroyed after 15 min idle or under memory pressure. Uses 512 KB stack (32-bit) or 2 MB (64-bit). Never moves between schedulers.
TaskThe unit of work a worker executesAssigned to an idle worker. Never moves between workers. Child tasks (e.g. parallel plans) can land on different workers.

Because SQLOS can spawn child tasks onto other workers, some schedulers can legitimately look busier than others — a worker may simply be holding more expensive tasks. Also note: tasks are handed to workers round-robin across NUMA nodes without regard to how many schedulers each node has, so an uneven scheduler split across NUMA nodes produces uneven work distribution.

StatesThe six states of a task

Normally you track tasks. The one exception is PENDING — a task that exists but hasn't been given a worker yet. Usually that's momentary and harmless, but a persistent backlog signals the dangerous condition of worker thread exhaustion (Chapter 13).

StateMeaningWhere it queues
RUNNINGCurrently executing on the scheduler— (max 1 per scheduler)
RUNNABLEReady to run, waiting for the scheduler / CPURUNNABLE queue
SUSPENDEDWaiting for an external event or resourceSUSPENDED queue
PENDINGCreated, waiting for an available worker—
SPINLOOPProcessing a spinlock — a synchronization object protecting an internal structure—
DONEComplete—

Spinlocks exist because SQL Server sometimes expects access to an object to be granted almost instantly, and burning a few CPU cycles in a loop is cheaper than a context switch.

The grocery store analogy

Cashiers = schedulers. Customers = tasks in the RUNNABLE queue. The customer being rung up = the RUNNING task. When an item is missing its UPC, the cashier sends someone for a price check and asks the customer to step aside — that's SUSPENDED. When the price comes back, the customer rejoins the back of the line — that's moving to the end of the RUNNABLE queue.

As the book notes, SQL Server is a lot more efficient than the store: a real customer sent to the back of the line after every price check would probably give up and go home.

4Wait Statistics — the core technique

Apart from startup and cleanup, a task just cycles between RUNNING, SUSPENDED, and RUNNABLE. Total elapsed time is the sum of all three.

The goal of tuning is to raise throughput by cutting query execution time — which means cutting time in one or more of those three states:

StateHow you reduce itValue in practice
RUNNINGFaster CPUs, more hardware — or do less work via query optimizationOptimization is usually far cheaper than hardware
RUNNABLEAdd CPU, or reduce system loadSymptom of CPU pressure
SUSPENDEDFix the contended resource (disk, locks, memory, network)Biggest win, most of the time

SQL Server tracks cumulative time spent in SUSPENDED, broken down by wait type, in sys.dm_os_wait_stats. That single view tells you what the system is waiting on more than anything else.

Listing 2-1 — Getting top wait types in the system (SQL Server 2012 and later)T-SQL
;WITH Waits
AS
(
  SELECT
    wait_type, wait_time_ms, waiting_tasks_count,signal_wait_time_ms
    ,wait_time_ms - signal_wait_time_ms AS resource_wait_time_ms
    ,100. * wait_time_ms / SUM(wait_time_ms) OVER() AS Pct
    ,100. * SUM(wait_time_ms) OVER(ORDER BY wait_time_ms DESC) /
        NULLIF(SUM(wait_time_ms) OVER(), 0) AS RunningPct
    ,ROW_NUMBER() OVER(ORDER BY wait_time_ms DESC) AS RowNum
  FROM sys.dm_os_wait_stats WITH (NOLOCK)
  WHERE
    wait_type NOT IN /* Filtering out nonessential system waits */
    (N'BROKER_EVENTHANDLER',N'BROKER_RECEIVE_WAITFOR',N'BROKER_TASK_STOP'
    ,N'BROKER_TO_FLUSH',N'BROKER_TRANSMITTER',N'CHECKPOINT_QUEUE',N'CHKPT'
    ,N'CLR_SEMAPHORE',N'CLR_AUTO_EVENT',N'CLR_MANUAL_EVENT'
    ,N'DBMIRROR_DBM_EVENT',N'DBMIRROR_EVENTS_QUEUE',N'DBMIRROR_WORKER_QUEUE'
    ,N'DBMIRRORING_CMD',N'DIRTY_PAGE_POLL',N'DISPATCHER_QUEUE_SEMAPHORE'
    ,N'EXECSYNC',N'FSAGENT',N'FT_IFTS_SCHEDULER_IDLE_WAIT',N'FT_IFTSHC_MUTEX'
    ,N'HADR_CLUSAPI_CALL',N'HADR_FILESTREAM_IOMGR_IOCOMPLETION'
    ,N'HADR_LOGCAPTURE_WAIT',N'HADR_NOTIFICATION_DEQUEUE'
    ,N'HADR_TIMER_TASK',N'HADR_WORK_QUEUE',N'KSOURCE_WAKEUP',N'LAZYWRITER_SLEEP'
    ,N'LOGMGR_QUEUE',N'ONDEMAND_TASK_QUEUE'
    ,N'PARALLEL_REDO_WORKER_WAIT_WORK',N'PARALLEL_REDO_DRAIN_WORKER'
    ,N'PARALLEL_REDO_LOG_CACHE',N'PARALLEL_REDO_TRAN_LIST'
    ,N'PARALLEL_REDO_WORKER_SYNC',N'PREEMPTIVE_SP_SERVER_DIAGNOSTICS'
    ,N'PREEMPTIVE_OS_LIBRARYOPS',N'PREEMPTIVE_OS_COMOPS', N'PREEMPTIVE_OS_PIPEOPS'
    ,N'PREEMPTIVE_OS_GENERICOPS',N'PREEMPTIVE_OS_VERIFYTRUST'
    ,N'PREEMPTIVE_OS_FILEOPS',N'PREEMPTIVE_OS_DEVICEOPS'
    ,N'PREEMPTIVE_OS_QUERYREGISTRY',N'PREEMPTIVE_XE_CALLBACKEXECUTE'
    ,N'PREEMPTIVE_XE_DISPATCHER',N'PREEMPTIVE_XE_GETTARGETSTATE'
    ,N'PREEMPTIVE_XE_SESSIONCOMMIT',N'PREEMPTIVE_XE_TARGETINIT'
    ,N'PREEMPTIVE_XE_TARGETFINALIZE',N'PWAIT_ALL_COMPONENTS_INITIALIZED'
    ,N'PWAIT_DIRECTLOGCONSUMER_GETNEXT',N'PWAIT_EXTENSIBILITY_CLEANUP_TASK'
    ,N'QDS_PERSIST_TASK_MAIN_LOOP_SLEEP',N'QDS_ASYNC_QUEUE'
    ,N'QDS_CLEANUP_STALE_QUERIES_TASK_MAIN_LOOP_SLEEP'
    ,N'REQUEST_FOR_DEADLOCK_SEARCH',N'RESOURCE_QUEUE',N'SERVER_IDLE_CHECK'
    ,N'SLEEP_BPOOL_FLUSH',N'SLEEP_DBSTARTUP',N'SLEEP_DCOMSTARTUP'
    ,N'SLEEP_MASTERDBREADY',N'SLEEP_MASTERMDREADY',N'SLEEP_MASTERUPGRADED'
    ,N'SLEEP_MSDBSTARTUP',N'SLEEP_SYSTEMTASK',N'SLEEP_TASK'
    ,N'SLEEP_TEMPDBSTARTUP',N'SNI_HTTP_ACCEPT',N'SOS_WORK_DISPATCHER'
    ,N'SP_SERVER_DIAGNOSTICS_SLEEP',N'SQLTRACE_BUFFER_FLUSH'
    ,N'SQLTRACE_INCREMENTAL_FLUSH_SLEEP',N'SQLTRACE_WAIT_ENTRIES'
    ,N'STARTUP_DEPENDENCY_MANAGER',N'WAIT_FOR_RESULTS'
    ,N'WAITFOR',N'WAITFOR_TASKSHUTDOWN',N'WAIT_XTP_HOST_WAIT'
    ,N'WAIT_XTP_OFFLINE_CKPT_NEW_LOG',N'WAIT_XTP_CKPT_CLOSE',N'WAIT_XTP_RECOVERY'
    ,N'XE_BUFFERMGR_ALLPROCESSED_EVENT',N'XE_DISPATCHER_JOIN',N'XE_DISPATCHER_WAIT'
    ,N'XE_LIVE_TARGET_TVF',N'XE_TIMER_EVENT')
)
SELECT
  w1.wait_type AS [Wait Type]
  ,w1.waiting_tasks_count AS [Wait Count]
  ,CONVERT(DECIMAL(12,3), w1.wait_time_ms / 1000.0) AS [Wait Time]
  ,CONVERT(DECIMAL(12,1), w1.wait_time_ms / w1.waiting_tasks_count)
        AS [Avg Wait Time]
  ,CONVERT(DECIMAL(12,3), w1.signal_wait_time_ms / 1000.0)
        AS [Signal Wait Time]
  ,CONVERT(DECIMAL(12,1), w1.signal_wait_time_ms / w1.waiting_tasks_count)
        AS [Avg Signal Wait Time]
  ,CONVERT(DECIMAL(12,3), w1.resource_wait_time_ms / 1000.0)
        AS [Resource Wait Time]
  ,CONVERT(DECIMAL(12,1), w1.resource_wait_time_ms / w1.waiting_tasks_count)
        AS [Avg Resource Wait Time]
  ,CONVERT(DECIMAL(6,3), w1.Pct)
        AS [Percent]
  ,CONVERT(DECIMAL(6,3), w1.RunningPct)
        AS [Running Percent]
FROM
    Waits w1
WHERE
    w1.RunningPct <= 99 OR w1.RowNum = 1
ORDER BY
    w1. RunningPct
OPTION (RECOMPILE, MAXDOP 1);

The NOT IN list filters out benign waits from internal SQL Server processes that spend most of their existence waiting on purpose. Every new SQL Server version adds wait types, so this list needs occasional maintenance.

How to read it in 20 seconds

Sort by total wait time, glance at the prefix of the top names: LCK_* → blocking · PAGEIOLATCH_* / WRITELOG / IO_COMPLETION → disk · RESOURCE_SEMAPHORE → memory grants · CXPACKET / CXPACKET-family → parallelism · ASYNC_NETWORK_IO → the client isn't consuming results fast enough. The Running Percent column tells you how many of the top rows you need before you've explained 80–90% of the time.

The methodWait Statistics Analysis

The cycle effectively never ends. That's fine — remember the Pareto principle: you get 80% of the improvement for 20% of the effort. Stop when further tuning stops being practical.

The trap: tunnel vision

Issues hide each other. The classic example: excessive disk waits are usually not caused by bad disks — they're caused by badly optimized queries that keep flushing the buffer pool and hammering the I/O subsystem. The book deliberately refuses to print a "wait type → root cause" lookup table, precisely so you don't chase symptoms instead of causes.

The crucial splitSignal waits vs. resource waits

Total wait time splits into two very different things:

  • Resource wait — time in the SUSPENDED queue, waiting for the resource itself (e.g. a disk page to arrive).
  • Signal wait — time in the RUNNABLE queue after the resource arrived, waiting for a CPU to pick it up.
Worked example

A task requests a data page. The I/O takes 6 ms. Then it waits 1 ms for a CPU to resume it. Result: 6 ms resource wait, 1 ms signal wait, 7 ms total.

Listing 2-2 — Signal versus resource waitsT-SQL
SELECT
    SUM(signal_wait_time_ms) AS [Signal Wait Time (ms)]
    ,CONVERT(DECIMAL(7,4), 100.0 * SUM (signal_wait_time_ms) /
        SUM(wait_time_ms)) AS [% Signal waits]
    ,SUM(wait_time_ms - signal_wait_time_ms) AS [Resource Wait Time (ms)]
    ,CONVERT (DECIMAL(7,4), 100.0 * sum(wait_time_ms - signal_wait_time_ms) /
        SUM(wait_time_ms)) AS [% Resource waits]
FROM
    sys.dm_os_wait_stats WITH (NOLOCK);
Threshold

Signal waits should not exceed 10–15% of total wait time. Higher suggests a CPU bottleneck with tasks piling up in the RUNNABLE queue. But don't automatically buy CPUs — query tuning may well solve it.

Sanity checksBefore you trust the numbers

  • Check the wait count, not just the total. A wait with a tiny waiting_tasks_count but a huge total time was probably one unusual event (an incident, a one-off), not a steady pattern. Deprioritize these early on.
  • Make sure the data is representative. Stats accumulate from the last restart, and workload changes over time. The book's usual request: clear waits a few days before starting the investigation.
  • DBCC SQLPERF('sys.dm_os_wait_stats', CLEAR) is safe in production, but it can disturb third-party monitoring tools that read the same counters. Alternative: take two snapshots and compute the delta (the book has a script for this in its companion materials).

5The DMVs you'll use every day

SQL Server ships with a huge number of dynamic management views. These are the handful the author reaches for constantly.

Server-widesys.dm_os_wait_stats

The aggregate view behind Wait Statistics: how many times each wait occurred, plus cumulative resource and signal time. Already covered above — this is the starting point of nearly every investigation.

Per sessionsys.dm_exec_session_wait_stats (2016+)

The same shape of data, but scoped to a single session. This is the tool for troubleshooting one slow query or stored procedure — it shows exactly what that session waited on, so you can pinpoint the bottleneck instead of guessing.

Two gotchas

Data clears when the session opens and when a pooled connection resets. And it isn't always updated for a statement that's still running — you generally need the query to finish before the numbers are complete.

Live snapshotsys.dm_os_waiting_tasks

Lists tasks currently sitting in the SUSPENDED queue. Perfect when the server is overloaded or unresponsive and you need to know why sessions are suspended right now — and it's the go-to for active blocking, because each row carries the blocker's session ID.

ColumnWhat it tells you
session_idWhich session is waiting
wait_typeWhat it's waiting for
wait_duration_msHow long it has been waiting
blocking_session_idWho is blocking it — the star of the show for blocking investigations
resource_addressWhich resource the task wants

You may see more than one row per session with parallel plans — each parallel worker shows up separately.

The workhorsesys.dm_exec_requests

A detailed, at-a-glance snapshot of every executing request. This is how you find the most CPU- or I/O-hungry query running right now.

  • Returns user and system sessions. Filter with session_id > 50 — though some system sessions now exceed 50, so for reliability join to sys.dm_exec_sessions and filter on is_user_process.
  • One row per session (unless you use MARS).
Column(s)What it gives you
session_idWhich session (one row each, unless MARS)
start_time, total_elapsed_timeWhen it started, and how long it's been going
statusRUNNING, RUNNABLE, SUSPENDED, or SLEEPING (an idle connection)
wait_type, wait_time, wait_resource, blocking_session_idPopulated when suspended — and blocking_session_id is again gold for blocking
cpu_time, logical_reads, reads, writes, granted_query_memory, dopExecution metrics — the evidence you need
sql_handle, plan_handleTo fetch the statement text and its execution plan
Listing 2-3 — Using the sys.dm_exec_requests viewT-SQL
SELECT
    er.session_id
    ,er.request_id
    ,DB_NAME(er.database_id) as [database]
    ,er.start_time
    ,CONVERT(DECIMAL(21,3),er.total_elapsed_time / 1000.) AS [duration]
    ,er.cpu_time
    ,SUBSTRING(
        qt.text,
        (er.statement_start_offset / 2) + 1,
            ((CASE er.statement_end_offset
                WHEN -1 THEN DATALENGTH(qt.text)
                ELSE er.statement_end_offset
            END - er.statement_start_offset) / 2) + 1
    ) AS [statement]
    ,er.status
    ,er.wait_type
    ,er.wait_time
    ,er.wait_resource
    ,er.blocking_session_id
    ,er.last_wait_type
    ,er.reads
    ,er.logical_reads
    ,er.writes
    ,er.granted_query_memory
    ,er.dop
    ,er.row_count
    ,er.percent_complete
    ,es.login_time
    ,es.original_login_name
    ,es.host_name
    ,es.program_name
    ,c.client_net_address
    ,ib.event_info AS [buffer]
    ,qt.text AS [sql]
    ,TRY_CONVERT(XML,p.query_plan) as [query_plan]
FROM
    sys.dm_exec_requests er WITH (NOLOCK)
        OUTER APPLY sys.dm_exec_input_buffer
            (er.session_id, er.request_id) ib
        OUTER APPLY sys.dm_exec_sql_text(er.sql_handle) qt
        OUTER APPLY
            sys.dm_exec_text_query_plan
            (
                er.plan_handle
                ,er.statement_start_offset
                ,er.statement_end_offset
            ) p
        LEFT JOIN sys.dm_exec_connections c WITH (NOLOCK) ON
            er.session_id = c.session_id
        LEFT JOIN sys.dm_exec_sessions es WITH (NOLOCK) ON
            er.session_id = es.session_id
WHERE
    er.status <> 'background' AND er.session_id > 50
ORDER BY
    er.cpu_time desc
OPTION (RECOMPILE, MAXDOP 1);

Version notes from the book: this needs SQL Server 2016 — drop the ep.dop column on older versions, and drop TRY_CONVERT before 2012.

Performance warning

Fetching an execution plan with sys.dm_exec_text_query_plan is expensive. If the server is already under heavy CPU load, comment that part out before you run this.

Occasionalsys.dm_os_schedulers

Not an everyday view, but two jobs: checking how schedulers are distributed across NUMA nodes (i.e. whether your affinity mask is right), and inspecting per-scheduler metrics. Chapter 1 had a basic version; here's the enhanced one:

Listing 2-4 — NUMA node scheduler statisticsT-SQL
SELECT
    parent_node_id AS [NUMA Node]
    ,COUNT(*) AS [Schedulers]
    ,SUM(IIF(status = N'VISIBLE ONLINE',1,0)) AS [Online Schedulers]
    ,SUM(IIF(status = N'VISIBLE OFFLINE',1,0)) AS [Offline Schedulers]
    ,SUM(current_tasks_count) AS [Current Tasks]
    ,SUM(runnable_tasks_count) AS [Runnable Tasks]
FROM
    sys.dm_os_schedulers WITH (NOLOCK)
WHERE
    status IN (N'VISIBLE ONLINE',N'VISIBLE OFFLINE')
GROUP BY
    parent_node_id
OPTION (RECOMPILE, MAXDOP 1);

current_tasks_count and runnable_tasks_count are the RUNNING and RUNNABLE queue depths per node. A big runnable_tasks_count hints at a CPU bottleneck — but this is an instantaneous reading, so don't over-interpret it. For trend data prefer cumulative measures: percentage of signal waits (Listing 2-2) or CPU load over time (Chapter 6).

6Resource Governor

An Enterprise Edition feature for segregating and throttling workloads on one server. The author calls it a niche feature — rarely seen in the field, and you could reasonably skip this section until you meet it. But always check whether it's configured on a server you're troubleshooting, because a wrong configuration can seriously cut throughput.

How it worksClassification → workload group → resource pool

At login, Resource Governor runs a classifier function — a simple user-defined function that inspects connection properties (login name, application name, client IP, etc.) and assigns the session to a workload group. Each group has limits such as MAXDOP, maximum CPU time per request, and maximum concurrent requests, and it's tied to a resource pool that controls actual resource usage.

Internal and Default are the two built-in groups/pools: Internal handles internal workload, Default catches everything unclassified. You can tune the Default group's parameters without creating any new groups at all — often enough for modest isolation.

LimitsWhat it can and can't control

ControllableNot controllable
CPU bandwidth and affinityBuffer pool usage — it's shared across all pools
Query memory grants (Chapter 7)True isolation — pools are not "virtual instances"
Disk throughput via IOPS limits (2014+)—
A definitional correction

Microsoft's docs call resource pools "the virtual SQL Server instances inside of a SQL Server instance." The author disagrees: pools don't provide enough isolation to deserve that description.

When to use it— and when not to

Good fits:

  • Separating different workloads inside a single database on a standalone server or a Failover Clustering instance
  • Reducing the impact of database maintenance — put backup compression or index maintenance in their own pool so they can't eat user sessions' CPU and I/O

Look elsewhere when:

  • You're on AlwaysOn Availability Groups — readable secondaries scale better long-term
  • You need to separate multiple databases on one instance — better to split them across instances, and probably virtualize
Real-world war story

The author once investigated a system where a major disk subsystem upgrade produced no performance improvement. Cause: I/O was being throttled by a leftover MAX_IOPS_PER_VOLUME setting in a resource pool. The hardware was fine; the configuration was strangling it.

Resource Governor isn't easy to configure or maintain — it needs planning and arithmetic across multiple busy pools, and the settings must be re-evaluated over time as hardware and workloads change.

7Key takeaways

SQLOS creates one scheduler per logical CPU and hands each a pool of workers. Tasks are assigned to workers, and workers voluntarily yield every 4 ms. While running, a task constantly migrates between RUNNING, SUSPENDED, and RUNNABLE.

SQL Server tracks time spent in each wait type and exposes it through sys.dm_os_waiting_tasks and sys.dm_os_wait_stats. Reading those, and finding the dominant waits, is Wait Statistics Analysis — one of the most-used troubleshooting techniques in the product.

The one warning

Don't jump to conclusions. Performance issues are often related and mask each other. Identifying the top wait is the start of the process, not the answer — you still have to confirm the root cause.
